config.title: The Brandenburg Gate, Before and After - FAQ
config.subtitle: Its history through five eras, what still stands there today, and how to visit.

items.q: Why is the Brandenburg Gate so famous?
items.a: It is the one Berlin landmark that has stood through the whole modern story of the city. Built in 1788 to 1791 as a royal city gate, it survived Napoleon carrying off its statue, near-total destruction in 1945, and nearly 30 years trapped behind the Berlin Wall. When it reopened on 22 December 1989 it became the picture of a reunited Germany. So it is famous less for how it looks and more for everything it has lived through in one spot.

items.q: Can you walk through the Brandenburg Gate, and is it free?
items.a: Yes. The Gate stands on Pariser Platz as an open public square, free and accessible at any hour, with no ticket and no queue. You can walk right up to the columns and through the central passage. The one thing worth knowing is that the middle passage was historically reserved for royalty; ordinary Berliners used the side arches, which is a nice detail to notice as you pass through.

items.q: What happened to the Brandenburg Gate in World War II?
items.a: It was heavily damaged but not destroyed. By 1945 almost every building around Pariser Platz had been flattened by bombing and the final battle, and the Gate remained one of the few recognisable structures in the ruined square. The Quadriga on top was wrecked, with just one horse's head surviving. East and West Berlin later restored the Gate together in 1956 to 1958 and recast the Quadriga from old moulds.

items.q: Was the Brandenburg Gate part of the Berlin Wall?
items.a: It ended up right inside it. When the Wall went up in 1961 the Gate was left in the death strip, the closed no-man's-land between East and West, so for nearly 30 years nobody could reach it from either side. It became the symbol of the divided city. It reopened on 22 December 1989, six weeks after the Wall fell. Today a double row of cobblestones set into the road nearby marks the exact line the Wall once followed.

items.q: What is the statue on top of the Brandenburg Gate?
items.a: It is the Quadriga, a chariot pulled by four horses and driven by a winged goddess of victory, made by Johann Gottfried Schadow and added in 1793. Napoleon took it to Paris as a trophy in 1806; Prussia recovered it in 1814 and added an iron cross and a Prussian eagle to the goddess's staff. The Quadriga faces east, looking down Unter den Linden into the heart of the old city rather than out toward the Tiergarten.

items.q: How do I get to the Brandenburg Gate?
items.a: Brandenburger Tor station is directly underneath the Gate, served by the S-Bahn (S1, S2, S25, S26) and the U5 underground line, so almost any central journey reaches it in a few minutes. On foot it sits at the western end of Unter den Linden, a straight and easy walk down from Museum Island and the TV Tower. It is one of the sights I point guests toward, though my own tour starts at Alexanderplatz rather than here.
